title: Consequences of climate change
competency: Examine the impacts of climate change on people, other life forms, water and forests.

keywords.def: A change that causes further change in the same direction, e.g. warming that releases CO₂ that causes more warming.

ideas.name: Where warming is fastest, and its effects

en.text: Models predict land will warm faster than the global average, especially the northern high latitudes in winter, as in Canada and Russia (greatest warming 2001–2006). Feedbacks can add to this: dark boreal forests absorb up to three times as much solar energy as snowy tundra, and warmer soils decompose faster and release more CO₂. More frequent heat waves increase heat-related deaths, while lower latitudes face more droughts and unpredictable rainfall.

en.text: Changes in precipitation may matter as much as temperature, and they are uneven: since the mid-twentieth century rain has increased over middle and high northern latitudes but decreased over some subtropical lands. The heaviest downpours are getting heavier, and even where the yearly total stays the same, rain may come in more intense wet spells with longer dry periods. Warmer soils dry out faster, making droughts worse and adding stress on agriculture and food security.

en.text: Sea level rises as land-based ice sheets and glaciers melt and as warming oceans expand, about half from each. Global sea level rose about 17 cm in the twentieth century and about 19 cm from 1900 to 2010; since 1993 it has risen about 3.4 cm per decade, roughly twice the twentieth-century rate. Rising seas put coastal and island communities at risk of flooding, raise storm surges, damage coral reefs and let saltwater into coastal groundwater.

en.text: In Antarctica warmer air may bring more snow inland while the coast melts; Greenland's ice sheet is expected to keep shrinking. Arctic sea ice hit record lows in 2007 and 2012 and may cover under 10 percent of the Arctic Ocean in summer by mid-century. More CO₂ can fertilize some plants, but crop yields may fall in the tropics while higher latitudes gain a longer growing season; overall, impacts on farming and ecosystems are expected to become increasingly negative. CO₂ in 2005 far exceeded the natural range of 180–300 ppm of the last 800,000 years, and shifting species affect human well-being.

notes.text: Figure 2.6 caption lists melting "sea ice" as a cause of sea-level rise; floating sea ice adds almost nothing. The rise comes from land ice plus thermal expansion, as the book's own text says (p.47).

p.49: the "2005 ... exceeds by far the natural range" sentence is from IPCC AR4 (2007, "650,000 years"), not AR5 (2013); the 2005 value (≈379 ppm) is not given; the bracket is not closed. These are observations, not "future impact".
p.46: "We can see that the greatest surface warming for 2001 to 2006..." refers to a map not printed in the book.
Feedback and Food security definitions, the sea-level rate steps and the floating-ice challenge are added.
